title: Threat Hunting with JA4/JA4S (+ Practical KQL Queries)
content_md: Threat Hunters, we usually look at IP addresses, domains and URLs. They are useful IOCs, but they can also change very quickly. TLS fingerprinting gives us another way to look at network activity. When an application starts a TLS connection, the client and server exchange information about how they will communicate, such as TLS versions, cipher suites and extensions. The way an application builds this communication can be used to create a TLS fingerprint. Instead of looking only at where a connection is going, JA fingerprints can help us understand how that connection is being established. JA3 vs JA4 JA3 fingerprints the TLS ClientHello and represents the result as an MD5 hash. JA4 follows the same idea but provides a more structured fingerprint. Part of the JA4 value can be read directly and includes information such as TLS version, number of cipher suites, extensions and ALPN. For Threat Hunting, this structure also allows us to analyze individual parts of the fingerprint instead of only searching for an exact hash. JA4S JA4S is the server-side companion to JA4. It was introduced by John Althouse and FoxIO in 2023 as part of the JA4+ network fingerprinting work. While JA4 fingerprints the TLS client, JA4S looks at the TLS server response/session. For Threat Hunting, the idea is simple: JA4 tells us something about who is connecting; JA4S tells us something about what is answering on the other side. This gives us another angle to hunt.
